title: The Spirit's Work and Sorrow Turned to Joy
summary: Jesus warns the disciples that they will be put out of the synagogues and even killed by people who think they are serving God. He tells them it is for their good that he goes away, because then he will send the Advocate, who will convict the world in regard to sin, righteousness, and judgment and guide the disciples into all truth. Using the picture of a woman in childbirth, he promises that their grief will turn to a joy no one can take away, and he ends by telling them that though they will have tribulation in the world, he has overcome the world.
story:
This is the last part of Jesus' teaching to the disciples before his prayer in chapter 17. Chapter 15 ended with the world's hatred and the joint witness of the Spirit and the disciples; chapter 16 makes the threat concrete and then answers it. The disciples are full of sorrow (verse 6), baffled by the phrase a little while (verses 16 to 19), and about to be scattered (verse 32). Jesus hides none of this. He tells them in advance so that they will not fall away (verse 1) and will remember, when the hour comes, that he told them (verse 4).

Against the threat he sets three gifts. The Spirit will come, and his coming depends on Jesus' going (verses 5 to 15). The disciples will see Jesus again, and their grief will turn to joy like a mother's after childbirth (verses 16 to 24), a promise first fulfilled on Easter evening, when the disciples rejoice at seeing the Lord (20:20). And they will have direct access to the Father, who loves them himself (verses 25 to 28). The chapter ends with the disciples' confident claim to understand, Jesus' warning that they will scatter and leave him alone, and his final word before the prayer: “take courage; I have overcome the world” (verse 33), spoken hours before what looks like complete defeat. After the prayer of chapter 17, the arrest follows immediately (18:1-12).
historical:
Jesus foresees two kinds of hostility (verse 2): exclusion from the synagogue and death at the hands of those who think they serve God. The Greek adjective aposynagōgos, put out of the synagogue, occurs only in John (9:22, 12:42, 16:2), and its history is disputed. J. Louis Martyn (History and Theology in the Fourth Gospel, 1968) linked it to the Birkat ha-Minim, the benediction against heretics that the Babylonian Talmud says was composed at Yavneh under Rabban Gamaliel II (b. Berakhot 28b-29a), and argued that John reflects a formal expulsion of his own community late in the first century. Reuven Kimelman (1981) and others have shown that the benediction's date, wording, and target are too uncertain to carry that conclusion, and Jonathan Bernier (Aposynagōgos and the Historical Jesus in John, 2013) argued that local exclusions of Jesus' followers are plausible in Jesus' own lifetime. Other early sources confirm that synagogue discipline fell on Jesus' followers: Luke 6:22 speaks of being excluded because of the Son of Man, Paul says he received the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine lashes five times (2 Corinthians 11:24), and in the second century Justin Martyr complains to a Jewish interlocutor that Christians are cursed in the synagogues (Dialogue with Trypho 16 and 96, around AD 155 to 160).

The second threat also came true in the first generation, and in the first instance both sides were Jews arguing about whether Jesus was Israel's Messiah. Saul of Tarsus persecuted the church out of zeal for God (Acts 8:1-3, 22:3-4, 26:9-11; Galatians 1:13-14; Philippians 3:6). Stephen was stoned (Acts 7:54-60); James the son of Zebedee was executed by Herod Agrippa I around AD 44 (Acts 12:1-2); and Josephus records that the high priest Ananus had James the brother of Jesus stoned in AD 62 (Antiquities 20.200). The thought that killing an apostate could be a service to God had deep roots in the story of Phinehas, whose zeal in killing an Israelite and a Midianite woman turned away God's wrath and won him a covenant of priesthood (Numbers 25:6-13; compare 1 Maccabees 2:23-26, where Mattathias kills an apostate Jew and is compared to Phinehas). A later midrash on that story says that whoever sheds the blood of the wicked is like one who offers a sacrifice (Numbers Rabbah 21:3, a medieval compilation drawing on older material).

There is a grave irony in later history. When the church gained power in the Roman Empire and in medieval Europe, Christians harassed and at times killed Jews in the belief that they served God, as in the massacres of Jewish communities in the Rhineland at Speyer, Worms, and Mainz by crusading bands in 1096. Jesus' warning about violence done in God's name applies to his own followers as surely as to anyone, and a faithful reading of verse 2 must name that reversal and refuse any use of the text to excuse contempt for Jewish people.
cultural:
Being put out of the synagogue meant more than missing a service. The synagogue was the center of a Jewish town's worship, teaching, charity, and local justice, and exclusion could cut a person off from family, marriage prospects, and trade. Forms of exclusion already existed: Ezra threatened those who ignored the assembly with forfeiture of property and separation from the congregation (Ezra 10:8), the Community Rule from Qumran sets out graded penalties of exclusion from the community's purity and meals (1QS 6:24 to 7:25), and the Mishnah knows a ban, niddui, imposed on those who defied the sages (m. Eduyot 5:6). The word Jesus uses for the persecutors' service (latreia) is the language of temple worship, which shows how sincerely they would believe they were right.

The picture of a woman in labor (verse 21) was a stock image in the prophets for sudden anguish and for the painful arrival of God's new age (Isaiah 26:17-19, 66:7-9; Jeremiah 30:6-7; Micah 4:9-10). One of the Thanksgiving Hymns from Qumran describes a woman in the throes of death bringing forth a male child, a wonderful counselor (1QHa 11:7-12), though scholars disagree whether it refers to a messianic figure or to the community. Later rabbinic tradition speaks of the birth pangs of the Messiah, the suffering that would precede his coming (b. Sanhedrin 98b), and the Synoptic Gospels call the troubles before the end the beginning of birth pains (Mark 13:8). In the ancient world childbirth was dangerous and often fatal (Rachel died in it, Genesis 35:16-19), so the image carries fear as well as hope. The phrase that a child (anthrōpos, a human being) is born into the world reflects a Hebrew idiom for being born.

Asking in Jesus' name (verses 23 and 24) draws on the ancient understanding of an agent. The Mishnah states the principle that a man's agent is as the man himself (m. Berakhot 5:5), so that to come in someone's name is to come with his authority and standing. The disciples will approach the Father as those who belong to Jesus. The contrast between figures of speech (paroimiai) and speaking plainly (parrēsia, verses 25 and 29) also had a social meaning. Parrēsia was the frank, open speech that Greek moralists prized in a true friend as opposed to a flatterer, a theme Plutarch treats in his essay How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend, and it fits the friendship Jesus has just described in 15:15.
literary:
The chapter alternates between warning and promise. It opens and closes with the same formula, I have told you these things (tauta lelalēka humin, verses 1 and 33, and again at 4, 6, and 25), so that the whole chapter presents itself as advance warning given in love. Its four sections are the coming persecution (1 to 4a), the Advocate's work (4b to 15), the puzzle of the little while (16 to 24), and plain speech and victory (25 to 33).

The Advocate sayings reach their fullest form here. The fourth saying (verses 7 to 11) is framed like a trial. The Spirit will convict (elenchei) the world, and each of the three charges is explained by a because clause. The world is guilty of sin because it does not believe in Jesus; it is wrong about righteousness because Jesus goes to the Father, whose acceptance vindicates the one the world condemned; and it is wrong about judgment because the prince of this world, who seemed to judge Jesus, has himself been condemned (compare 12:31). The fifth saying (verses 12 to 15) turns from the world to the disciples: the Spirit will guide them into all the truth, speaking what he hears, as Jesus spoke what he heard from the Father (8:26), and he will glorify Jesus by taking what is his and declaring it. The chain Father to Son to Spirit to disciples is set out in a few lines.

The phrase a little while (mikron) appears seven times in verses 16 to 19, and the disciples' repetition of Jesus' words, their muttering to one another, and his reply that repeats them again, slow the narrative almost to a halt so that the reader feels their confusion. The labor image then resolves it. Two contrasting pairs structure verses 20 to 22: you will weep and the world will rejoice; your grief will turn to joy, and no one will take it away. The closing exchange is full of irony. The disciples claim that now at last Jesus speaks plainly and that they believe (verses 29 and 30); Jesus answers with a question that can be read as a question or a statement, Do you now believe, and warns that an hour is coming, and has come, when they will be scattered (verse 32). The scattering recalls Zechariah 13:7, which the other Gospels quote at this point (Mark 14:27). The last sentence gathers the Gospel's language into a single contrast: in Me, peace; in the world, tribulation; and over both, I have overcome the world.

outline.t: A little while: grief turned to joy
Plain speech, scattering, and victory over the world

doctrines.note: The Spirit's coming depends on Jesus' going (verse 7). Toward the world he acts as prosecutor, convicting it in regard to sin, righteousness, and judgment (verses 8 to 11); toward the disciples he is guide and interpreter, leading them into all the truth, speaking what he hears, and declaring what is to come (verse 13). His work is to glorify Jesus, not himself (verse 14).

Jesus has more to say than the disciples can bear (verse 12), and the Spirit will guide them into all the truth by taking what belongs to Jesus and declaring it (verses 13 to 15). The church has read this as the promise behind the apostolic witness and the New Testament. What the Spirit discloses is not a new message beside Christ but what is his, so that the test of any claim to revelation is whether it glorifies him.

The world's verdict on Jesus is reversed. The Spirit shows that the real sin is unbelief, that the righteous one is the man the world condemned, whom the Father receives, and that the one condemned is “the prince of this world” (verse 11). Judgment in John is already under way at the cross (12:31), before its final form at the last day.

After the resurrection the disciples will ask the Father in Jesus' name and receive, so that their joy may be complete (verses 23 and 24). Jesus adds that he will not need to ask the Father on their behalf, “For the Father Himself loves you” (verse 27). Prayer in his name is not persuading a reluctant Father through a go-between; it is the access of those whom the Father already loves because they belong to his Son.

Jesus promises his followers exclusion, death at the hands of the sincere, grief while the world rejoices, and tribulation in the world (verses 2, 20, and 33). He does not explain suffering away; he places it within a story that ends in joy no one can take away, like the anguish of labor forgotten at a birth (verse 21), and he grounds courage in his own victory.

words.note: Aposynagōgos, put out of the synagogue, excluded. The word occurs only three times, all in John (9:22, 12:42, 16:2), and nowhere in earlier Greek literature, so it may have been coined for this situation. In chapter 9 it is the threat that silences the blind man's parents, in chapter 12 the fear that keeps some leaders from confessing their faith, and here a prediction for the disciples. Its date and scope are debated (see the historical note), but in each case it names the cost of confessing Jesus as Messiah within the Jewish community of the time.

Latreia, worship, service to God. It occurs five times in the New Testament (John 16:2; Romans 9:4, 12:1; Hebrews 9:1, 9:6), always of religious service, and in the Greek Old Testament it names the Passover service and the worship of the tabernacle (Exodus 12:25-26). Jesus says that those who kill his followers will think they are offering latreia to God. The word shows that the danger he names is not cynical cruelty but sincere religious zeal turned to violence.

Elenchō, to convict, expose, prove wrong, reprove. It occurs 17 times in the New Testament and three in John (3:20, 8:46, 16:8). BDAG gives senses ranging from bringing to light and exposing, to convincing someone of wrongdoing, to reproving. In 3:20 evildoers avoid the light so their deeds will not be exposed; in 8:46 Jesus asks who can convict him of sin. In 16:8 the Spirit brings the world's guilt to light, whether or not the world accepts the verdict, which is why translations vary between convict, convince, and prove wrong.

Hodēgeō, to lead the way, guide. It occurs five times in the New Testament (Matthew 15:14, Luke 6:39, John 16:13, Acts 8:31, Revelation 7:17). The Ethiopian official uses it when he asks how he can understand Isaiah unless someone guides him (Acts 8:31), and in the Greek Psalms it is used of God's leading, as in Psalm 25:5 (24:5 in the Greek numbering), where the psalmist asks to be led in God's truth. The Spirit's work is pictured as leading travelers along a road into the truth that Jesus is (14:6).

Lupē, grief, sorrow, pain. It occurs 16 times in the New Testament, four in this chapter (verses 6, 20, 21, 22). It covers both mental distress and physical pain, which suits verse 21, where the same word names a mother's pain in labor and the disciples' grief at Jesus' going. Jesus does not tell the disciples their grief is wrong; he tells them it will be turned (genēsetai) into joy, the grief itself becoming the way to the joy, as the labor becomes the birth.

Paroimia, a proverb, figure of speech, veiled saying. It occurs five times in the New Testament: at 10:6 of the shepherd discourse, three times in this chapter (verses 25 twice and 29), and in 2 Peter 2:22 of a proverb. In the Greek Old Testament it is the title of the book of Proverbs. Jesus contrasts such figurative speech with parrēsia, plain and open speech, and says the hour is coming when he will speak of the Father plainly. The disciples think that hour has arrived (verse 29), but full understanding waits for the resurrection and the Spirit.

Thlipsis, pressure, affliction, tribulation. It occurs about 45 times in the New Testament but only twice in John, both in this chapter: of a mother's anguish in labor (verse 21) and of the disciples' trouble in the world (verse 33). The word first meant physical pressing or crushing and came to mean distress of every kind; Paul uses it often of his own sufferings (2 Corinthians 1:4-8), and Revelation of the great tribulation (7:14). The pairing in this chapter suggests that the church's affliction is also a kind of labor that ends in joy.

Nikaō, to conquer, overcome, prevail. It occurs 28 times in the New Testament: once in John's Gospel (16:33), six times in 1 John, and 17 times in Revelation. The perfect tense in “I have overcome the world” presents the victory as accomplished and standing, spoken before the cross as if already done. 1 John picks up the word: the one who overcomes the world is the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God (1 John 5:4-5), and in Revelation the Lamb overcomes by being slain (5:5-6).

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus facing death with sovereign calm. He calls his going a return to the one who sent him (verses 5 and 28), speaks of it as for the disciples' good (verse 7), and announces his victory before the battle (verse 33). Verse 28 compresses the whole shape of his mission into a single sentence: he came from the Father and entered the world, and he is leaving the world and going to the Father. That descent and ascent frames the Gospel from its prologue (1:1-14) to his words to Mary Magdalene (20:17), and the rest of the New Testament confesses it in similar terms (Philippians 2:6-11).

He is also the one who sends the Spirit (verse 7), which the Old Testament reserves to God. The prophets promised that God would pour out his Spirit in the last days (Joel 2:28-29, Ezekiel 36:26-27), and John the Baptist had identified Jesus as the one who would baptize with the Holy Spirit (1:33). Everything that belongs to the Father is his (verse 15), and the Spirit's work is to glorify him (verse 14). Here the doctrine of the Trinity is not stated in the later creeds' vocabulary, but its shape is visible: the Father gives, the Son possesses and sends, the Spirit receives and declares.

The images of the chapter point to the passion and resurrection. The scattering of the disciples and the Son left alone (verse 32) recall the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered in Zechariah 13:7, which the other Gospels quote on this same night (Mark 14:27, Matthew 26:31). Yet Jesus is not alone, because the Father is with him, a word that stands in quiet tension with the cry of dereliction in Mark 15:34 and that John leaves unresolved. The woman in labor echoes Isaiah 26 and 66, where Zion's anguish gives birth to a new people, and it prepares for the resurrection appearances, where the disciples' grief does turn to joy (20:20). The victory over the world is the victory of one who is about to be lifted up on a cross, which John has already called the judgment of this world and the casting out of its ruler (12:31-32).
interpretation:
The fathers read the chapter chiefly for its teaching on the Spirit. Augustine's Tractates on John 93 to 103 cover it. In Tractate 95 he wrestled with the difficult verses 8 to 11, and in Tractates 96 and 97 he warned against those who used verse 12, things you cannot yet bear, to justify teachings the apostles never gave. John Chrysostom (Homilies 78 and 79 on John) dwelt on why it was to the disciples' advantage that Jesus go away and on the comfort he gave them in their grief. Cyril of Alexandria, whose Commentary on John reaches this chapter in its tenth and eleventh books, used verses 14 and 15 to argue that the Spirit belongs to the Son's own being and not only to the Father, and Western theologians drew on the same verses in support of the filioque.

The promise of the Paraclete was also claimed by others. In the second century Montanus and his prophetesses in Phrygia announced a New Prophecy in which the Paraclete spoke through them, and Epiphanius (Panarion 48) records sayings in which Montanus seems to speak as the Paraclete himself; Tertullian later joined the movement. In the third century Mani, the founder of Manichaeism, presented himself as the Paraclete promised by Jesus. From the eighth century some Muslim writers identified the promised Advocate with Muhammad, connecting the promise with the Qur'an's statement that Jesus foretold a messenger named Ahmad (Qur'an 61:6). Ibn Ishaq's biography of the Prophet (he died about 767) quotes John 15:23-16:1 in an Arabic version that renders the Paraclete with a Christian Palestinian Aramaic word, Munahhemana, the comforter, which later readers heard as echoing Muhammad's name; the historian Sean Anthony has traced how that translation was made. Christian writers from the early Middle Ages onward replied that the Paraclete is identified in the text itself as the Spirit of truth, sent in Jesus' name, whom the world cannot see and who dwells in the disciples (14:17, 14:26).

The Reformers read verses 8 to 11 as a description of the Spirit's work through preaching, convicting consciences of unbelief and pointing them to Christ's righteousness, and Martin Luther preached through chapters 14 to 16 in the late 1530s. Modern scholarship has continued to find verses 8 to 11 among the hardest in the Gospel. D. A. Carson (The Function of the Paraclete in John 16:7-11, Journal of Biblical Literature, 1979) argued that each clause exposes the world's own sin, its false righteousness, and its false judgment. Martyn's two-level reading of the Gospel (1968) made verse 2 a window on the Johannine community, and Jewish scholars such as Adele Reinhartz (Cast Out of the Covenant, 2018) have asked Christian readers to face how the chapter's language has been heard.

The chapter was the backbone of the Easter season in the historic Western lectionary: 16:16-23 on Jubilate (the third Sunday after Easter), 16:5-15 on Cantate (the fourth), 16:23-30 on Rogate (the fifth, before the Rogation days of prayer), and 15:26 to 16:4 on Exaudi (the Sunday after the Ascension). Those assignments shaped the church music of Lutheran Leipzig. Johann Sebastian Bach wrote cantatas on these Gospels, among them Ihr werdet weinen und heulen (BWV 103, 1725) on verse 20, Es ist euch gut, dass ich hingehe (BWV 108, 1725) on verse 7, Wahrlich, wahrlich, ich sage euch (BWV 86, 1724) and Bisher habt ihr nichts gebeten in meinem Namen (BWV 87, 1725) on verses 23 and 24, and two settings of Sie werden euch in den Bann tun (BWV 44, 1724, and BWV 183, 1725) on verse 2. The Revised Common Lectionary reads 15:26-27 with 16:4b-15 on the Day of Pentecost in Year B and 16:12-15 on Trinity Sunday in Year C.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from manuscripts. In verse 13 the manuscripts are divided between guiding into all the truth (eis tēn alētheian pasan) and guiding in all the truth (en tē alētheia pasē); the Westcott and Hort edition printed the first and the current Nestle-Aland text prints the second, though the meaning is nearly the same. At the end of verse 16 the King James Version adds ‘because I go to the Father’, a clause the earliest manuscripts lack; it was probably added from verse 17, where the disciples quote it. In verse 22 manuscripts differ between no one takes (present) and no one will take (future) your joy. In verse 23 the phrase in My name stands in different places in different manuscripts, attached either to the asking, as in the BSB and KJV, or to the giving, as in the RSV's ‘he will give it to you in my name’. In verse 27 some manuscripts read that you believed I came from the Father rather than from God.

There are also translation differences. The verb in verse 8 (elenchō) is rendered ‘reprove’ (KJV), ‘convict’ (ESV, BSB), and ‘prove the world wrong’ (NRSV), reflecting a real question about whether the Spirit convicts the world so that it sees its guilt or exposes its guilt whether it sees it or not. The KJV's ‘Comforter’ in verse 7 is the same word modern versions render ‘Advocate’, ‘Helper’, or ‘Counselor’. In verse 31 the Greek can be punctuated as a question, Do you now believe? (BSB, ESV), or as a statement, ‘Now you believe’, which some commentators prefer.

teach.big: Jesus' going to the Father, which looks like loss, is the gift that brings the Spirit, turns grief into lasting joy, and gives his troubled people peace in him because he has already overcome the world.

outline.t: Jesus tells his followers the cost in advance so that suffering will confirm his word rather than shake their faith, and he names sincere religious violence as a real danger.
What feels like loss can be for our good: the Son's going is the condition of the Spirit's coming.
The Spirit reverses the world's verdict on Jesus, exposing unbelief as sin, vindicating the crucified as righteous, and showing that the devil, not Jesus, stands condemned.
The Spirit leads Christ's people into the truth by taking what is Christ's and declaring it, so the Spirit's work always glorifies Jesus.
Jesus meets his disciples' confusion with patience, knowing their questions before they ask them.
Christian grief is real but not final; like labor pains it gives way to a joy that no one can take away.
The resurrection opens a new kind of prayer: asking the Father directly in Jesus' name, so that joy may be complete.
The Father himself loves those who love his Son, and the whole mission of Jesus is summed up in his coming from the Father and returning to him.
Our confidence fails, but his does not: the disciples will scatter, yet Jesus gives peace in himself because he has overcome the world.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misuses of this chapter are common. The first treats verse 13 as a promise that the Spirit will give individual Christians new doctrines or private revelations beyond Scripture. The promise was given first to the apostles, and its content is what belongs to Christ (verses 14 and 15); claims that do not glorify Jesus or that contradict what he said fail the test he sets. The opposite error treats the Spirit's guidance as having ended so completely that believers expect nothing of him now, when the chapter presents the Spirit as the continuing presence of Christ's teaching with his people.

The second pitfall makes verses 8 to 11 a technique for inducing guilt, as though preaching must make people feel as bad as possible before offering grace. The conviction belongs to the Spirit, and its content is not general moral failure but unbelief in Jesus and a false verdict on him. The third pitfall reads verses 23 and 24 as a formula, so that ending a prayer with in Jesus' name guarantees the answer. To ask in his name is to ask as one who belongs to him and seeks what he seeks, as the parallel in 15:7 and 1 John 5:14 make plain. The fourth misreads verse 33 as a promise that faithful Christians will be spared tribulation, or, conversely, as a call to seek it. Jesus promises tribulation and peace together, and his victory does not remove the trouble but defeats its power to have the last word.

Finally, verses 1 to 4 have been misused in two directions. Christians have read them as a verdict on Jews as persecutors, forgetting that the disciples were Jews and that Christians later did the same things to Jews. And they have used them to treat any opposition as persecution, when Jesus speaks of hostility that comes because they have not known the Father or him (verse 3).
teach.pastoral: This chapter speaks directly to grief. Verses 20 to 22 do not tell mourners to stop weeping, and teachers should not use them that way. Jesus says that his friends will weep and wail, that the world may rejoice while they grieve, and that joy will come after, not instead of, the grief. The labor image fits the experience of many who have lost someone: the anguish is real and bodily. Handle it with care in a room that may include women who have lost a child in pregnancy or childbirth or who long for a child, for whom the image of a mother forgetting her anguish may be painful rather than consoling; the point is the promise of joy, not a claim that every grief ends in birth. For those who feel abandoned by friends in a crisis, verse 32 offers company: Jesus knew what it was to be left alone, and he found the Father with him. For people who have suffered at the hands of sincere religious people, including those abused by church leaders who thought they were serving God, verse 2 is a sober recognition that religious conviction can be turned to harm, and that Jesus saw it coming and stands with the victims, not the zealots.

hard.q: Who is the Advocate, and does his coming mean new revelation beyond what Jesus taught?
hard.a:
The strongest challenges to the Christian reading have come from those who claimed the promise for someone else. Montanus in the second century announced that the Paraclete now spoke through him and his prophetesses, and Tertullian found the claim persuasive enough to join the movement. Mani in the third century presented himself as the promised Paraclete. From the eighth century onward many Muslim scholars, beginning with the Arabic version of John 15:23-16:1 in Ibn Ishaq's biography of the Prophet, identified the Advocate with Muhammad, often linking the Greek paraklētos to periklytos, ‘praised one’, and so to the name Ahmad in Qur'an 61:6. All these readings take seriously what the chapter says: that Jesus had much more to say (verse 12), that someone would come after him, and that this one would declare what is to come (verse 13).

Christian responses begin with the text. No Greek manuscript reads periklytos, and the chapter identifies the Advocate as the Spirit of truth (verse 13; compare 14:17 and 14:26), sent by Jesus (verse 7), whom the world cannot see and who will be in the disciples (14:17), who speaks not on his own but what he hears and glorifies Jesus by taking what is his (verses 13 and 14). The historian Sean Anthony has shown that Ibn Ishaq's Arabic depends on a Christian Palestinian Aramaic Gospel that rendered paraklētos as Munahhemana, the comforter, a word later heard as an echo of Muhammad's name. Anti-Montanist writers whose arguments Eusebius preserves (Ecclesiastical History 5.16 to 18) rejected the New Prophecy's claims, and the church came to read the promise as fulfilled when the Spirit was given to the apostles (20:22, Acts 2).

Among Christians themselves the question is how the Spirit's guidance continues. Many Protestants hold that the promise of verse 13 was given to the apostles and fulfilled in the apostolic witness preserved in the New Testament, and that the Spirit now illuminates that witness rather than adding to it; the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 1) says that nothing is to be added to Scripture by new revelations of the Spirit. The Catholic and Orthodox churches hold that the Spirit guides the whole church, preserving and unfolding apostolic truth through its tradition, councils, and teaching office, as the Second Vatican Council's Dei Verbum (1965) describes. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians affirm that the Spirit still speaks through gifts such as prophecy, while most insist that such words are tested by Scripture and never equal to it (1 Thessalonians 5:19-21). All agree on the test Jesus gives: the Spirit glorifies Christ and declares what is his. How that guidance relates to Scripture and to the church's teaching is a second-order question on which faithful Christians disagree.

hard.q: Were Jesus' followers really expelled from synagogues and killed, and has this verse fed Christian hostility toward Jews?
hard.a:
The historical objection is that verse 2 describes the situation of John's community decades later, not anything Jesus could have foreseen in AD 30. J. Louis Martyn (History and Theology in the Fourth Gospel, 1968) argued that the language of being put out of the synagogue reflects a formal decision late in the first century, and many critical scholars have followed him in reading the verse as the Johannine community's experience placed on Jesus' lips. The ethical objection is sharper. Jewish scholars, among them Adele Reinhartz (Cast Out of the Covenant, 2018), point out that Christians have read verses like this as proof that Jews are persecutors by nature, and that for most of Christian history it was Jews who were expelled, forcibly converted, and killed by Christians who thought they served God. On this view the verse has done harm whatever its origin.

On the history, Reuven Kimelman (1981) and others have shown that the benediction against heretics cannot be securely dated to John's time or shown to have targeted Christians, which weakens the main support for Martyn's late dating, and Jonathan Bernier (Aposynagōgos and the Historical Jesus in John, 2013) argued that local synagogue exclusions of Jesus' followers are plausible in Jesus' lifetime, since Jewish communities already practiced forms of exclusion (Ezra 10:8, 1QS 6:24 to 7:25). Other first-century evidence shows synagogue discipline and lethal violence against Jesus' followers within a few years of his death: the stoning of Stephen, Saul's campaign, Paul's floggings (2 Corinthians 11:24), and the execution of the two Jameses. A prophet who had seen the fate of John the Baptist and expected his own death could foresee that his followers would share it. Historians will weigh these arguments differently, and Christians who hold a high view of the Gospel's truthfulness are found on both sides of the question whether John's wording also reflects later experience.

On the ethical question, the text itself resists misuse. Jesus and his disciples are Jews, and the verse warns against a danger in every religious community, not a trait of one people; the same zeal drove Saul, a Pharisee who became an apostle. The church's own history fulfills the warning with Christians as the persecutors, from the Rhineland massacres of 1096 to Martin Luther's On the Jews and Their Lies (1543). The Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate (1965) and statements by many Protestant churches since have repudiated the teaching of contempt. A faithful reader holds both truths: the early disciples did suffer for confessing Jesus, and the verse must never become a warrant for making anyone else suffer.

observe: What two things does Jesus say will happen to the disciples in verse 2, and why does he say he is telling them now (verses 1 and 4)?
What three things will the Advocate convict the world about, and what reason is given for each (verses 8 to 11)?
What do the disciples claim in verses 29 and 30, and how does Jesus answer them (verses 31 to 33)?
interpret: Why would it be better for the disciples that Jesus go away (verse 7)? What could the Spirit do that Jesus' bodily presence did not?
What does the picture of a woman in labor teach about the relationship between the disciples' grief and their joy?
What does it mean to ask the Father in Jesus' name, and how is that different from using his name as a formula?
apply: Where has sincere religious conviction, your own or others', turned harsh or cruel? How can a person guard against that?
What grief are you carrying now, and what would it mean to hold it within Jesus' promise that joy will come after it?
Jesus promises both tribulation in the world and peace in him. Which of the two do you tend to forget, and what difference would remembering it make?
